opus-5.5.text:
I think the analogy works on a few levels.

First, SpaceX started with a goal that sounded almost absurd: make humanity multiplanetary. That north star shapes every engineering decision, even the boring ones. For us the north star is building an AI mathematician, a system that can reason rigorously, prove new theorems, and eventually help discover mathematics humans haven't reached. Once you take that goal seriously, it changes how you build everything below it.

Second, SpaceX succeeded by being vertically integrated. They didn't just buy parts and assemble them; they rebuilt the stack because the existing supply chain wasn't designed for what they wanted. AI for math is similar. You can't just take a general-purpose language model and ask it nicely to do research mathematics. You need formal verification, which in practice means languages like Lean. You need data that barely exists, because most mathematics was never written in machine-checkable form. You need new training methods where the verifier acts as a reward signal. So we have to build the data engine, the models, and the verification infrastructure together.

Third is reusability, the thing that made rockets economically viable. In mathematics, the equivalent is that formally verified knowledge compounds. Once a lemma is proven in Lean, it's correct forever and every future proof can build on it. Each result lowers the cost of the next one, which is exactly the flywheel you want.

And finally, there's the near-term-versus-long-term structure. SpaceX funded the Mars dream by launching satellites and resupplying the space station, things with real customers today. We think about it the same way. Verified reasoning has very concrete applications now: chip design verification, software correctness, safety-critical systems, anywhere you need guarantees rather than just plausible answers. Those applications keep the company grounded while we work toward the bigger goal.

So it's a moonshot, but an engineering moonshot, not a speculative one. The path is hard, but you can see the steps.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the SpaceX analogy comes down to one thing: the gap between what everyone agrees is theoretically possible and what anyone has actually been willing to build. When Elon started SpaceX, the physics of reusable rockets was not in question. The equations were in textbooks. What was missing was someone willing to say, we are going to treat this as an engineering problem with a very long horizon, accept that the first several attempts will blow up, and keep going because the payoff is a fundamentally different cost curve.

Mathematics is in a similar place right now. Formal verification tools like Lean exist. We know how to make a machine check a proof with certainty. We know large models can generate candidate reasoning. Nobody disputes that a system could, in principle, propose a proof and have it verified end to end without a human in the loop. But almost everyone treats that as a far-off research curiosity, because the serious version of it is unglamorous. You have to formalize enormous libraries of existing mathematics. You have to build infrastructure for the model to search, fail, and learn from a verifier that says no ten thousand times before it says yes. It is not a demo you make in a weekend.

So the SpaceX part, for me, is twofold. First, it is about betting that the cost of a verified mathematical result can drop by orders of magnitude, the way launch cost did, and that when it does, the demand side changes completely. Right now mathematics is bottlenecked on a very small number of extremely talented people. If a correct proof becomes cheap and fast, you don't just do the same mathematics faster. You start asking questions that were never worth asking because the labor cost was prohibitive. Chip verification, cryptography, safety proofs for software, and also pure mathematics where a conjecture sits untouched for decades because nobody has the time.

Second, it is about doing this as a company rather than purely as academic research. I love academia, I come from it, but the incentive structure there rewards a paper, not a reliable system that keeps running at scale. Rockets needed a company that was willing to be judged on whether the thing actually lands. I think mathematical AI needs the same thing. We want to be judged on whether the proof actually checks.

And frankly, there is also the part where people told Elon he was crazy to think a private company could compete with national space programs. I hear a version of that quite often, that mathematics is the last fortress of human intellect, that machines will never truly contribute. I am genuinely humble about the difficulty. But I would rather be the one building the rocket and watching it explode a few times than the one explaining afterward why it was obviously going to work.

astra-6.text:
The analogy, for me, is about having a clear, ambitious destination that forces you to solve hard engineering problems along the way. For AI and mathematics, that destination is a system that can help discover new mathematics—not just answer questions whose solutions we already know.

But you don’t get there in one leap. You need intermediate milestones: can the system reason reliably, check its arguments, and become useful to mathematicians? Those capabilities have value as you build toward the larger goal. That’s the sense in which I see the SpaceX comparison: a long-term scientific ambition pursued through concrete engineering progress.

sol-6.1.text:
The analogy is about taking a long-term scientific ambition and building an engineering path toward it. For us, that ambition is AI that can do original mathematical research. You don’t get there in one leap. You need concrete milestones, a team that brings research and engineering together, and a tight feedback loop where each attempt teaches you something.

And mathematics is a particularly exciting place to do that because you can check whether a proof is correct. That gives you a way to measure progress toward a very ambitious goal. So the SpaceX comparison is really about the approach: take the big goal seriously, then make it concrete enough to build toward.
